title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather — Germany's number one conversation starter — and link two sentences with *und*, *aber*, *oder*, *denn*.
bekal: describe the weather and the seasons
use *es* as an empty subject (*Es regnet*)
name clothes for each kind of weather

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Typisch deutsches Wetter
dialogs.intro: November in Berlin. Budi has just come in from outside, soaked to the skin, and discovers that complaining about the weather is a national sport.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Oh je, du bist ja ganz nass! Regnet es wieder?
lines.id: Oh dear, you're completely soaked! Is it raining again?
lines.literal: oh dear, you are indeed completely wet! rains it again?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, es regnet seit heute Morgen. Und es ist sehr windig.
lines.id: Yes, it's been raining since this morning. And it's really windy.
lines.literal: yes, it rains since today morning. and it is very windy.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Typisch November. Wie ist das Wetter in Indonesien?
lines.id: Typical November. What's the weather like in Indonesia?
lines.literal: typical November. how is the weather in Indonesia?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Warm, immer warm. Es gibt nur zwei Jahreszeiten: trocken und nass.
lines.id: Warm, always warm. There are only two seasons: dry and wet.
lines.literal: warm, always warm. it gives only two year-times: dry and wet.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Kein Winter? Das kann ich mir nicht vorstellen.
lines.id: No winter? I can't imagine that.
lines.literal: no winter? that can I me not imagine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Und ich kann mir keinen Schnee vorstellen. Wie kalt wird es hier?
lines.id: And I can't imagine snow. How cold does it get here?
lines.literal: and I can me no snow imagine. how cold becomes it here?

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Im Januar oft minus fünf Grad. Manchmal minus zehn.
lines.id: In January it's often minus five degrees. Sometimes minus ten.
lines.literal: in-the January often minus five degree. sometimes minus ten.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Minus zehn! Dann bleibe ich zu Hause.
lines.id: Minus ten! Then I'm staying at home.
lines.literal: minus ten! then stay I at home.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Das geht nicht, denn im Winter ist es hier oft schön.
lines.id: That won't do, because winter here is often beautiful.
lines.literal: that goes not, because in-the winter is it here often beautiful.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Kalt, aber sonnig. Du brauchst nur eine gute Jacke.
lines.id: Cold, but sunny. You just need a good jacket.
lines.literal: cold, but sunny. you need only a good jacket.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dann kaufe ich morgen eine Jacke oder ich fliege nach Hause.
lines.id: Then tomorrow I'll buy a jacket or I'll fly home.
lines.literal: then buy I tomorrow a jacket or I fly home.

notes: ***es* as an empty subject.** *Es regnet*, *Es schneit*, *Es ist kalt* — the word *es* doesn't point to anything; it just fills the subject slot, which must always be filled in German. It's exactly the "it" in English "it's raining".

**Line 9: *denn im Winter ist es…*** The word *denn* ("because") links two sentences **without changing the word order**. Compare *weil*, which you'll learn in unit 20 and which sends the verb to the end. For now, *denn* is the easiest way to give a reason.
***wird* comes from *werden*** ("to become"). *Wie kalt wird es?* = "how cold does it get?". This verb will be very useful in A2; here, just recognize the form *es wird*.
**Temperatures use *Grad*, with no plural**: *fünf Grad*, *minus zehn Grad*. Germany uses Celsius for everything, and the question is *Wie viel Grad sind es?*
***typisch*** is used just like English "typical": *typisch November*, *typisch deutsch*. It's often said in an affectionately complaining tone.

***Oh je!*** is a small cry of sympathy, like "oh dear". Its neighbors: *Ach so!* ("oh, I see"), *Na ja…* ("well…"), *Genau!* ("exactly"). These four will make your German sound far more alive than any perfect sentence.

grammars.title: es — the subject that points to no one
body: Every German sentence must have a subject. When there's no real one — weather, time, general situations — the slot is filled with *es*.
after: Look at the last two rows: *es gibt* and *wie geht es dir* use the same *es*. Once you see it as one habit of the language — not seven separate rules — none of it feels strange anymore.
⚠️ *Es* can't be dropped, even when it sounds unnecessary. *Regnet* on its own isn't a sentence — just as English needs "it" in "it's raining".

grammars.title: Linking two sentences
body: The four linking words below share one feature that makes them much easier than other conjunctions: **they don't count as position one**. The sentence after them is built exactly like a stand-alone sentence.

head: Conjunction
Meaning
Example
rows: Es ist kalt, **aber** es ist sonnig.
Ich kaufe eine Jacke **oder** ich bleibe zu Hause.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, **denn** es regnet.

after: Compare these two carefully: *…, **denn** es **regnet**.* and *…, **weil** es **regnet**.* The first uses normal word order; the second — which you'll learn in unit 20 — sends the verb to the end. Exactly the same meaning, completely different structure.

**Commas:** *aber*, *denn* and *sondern* always have a comma before them. *Und* and *oder* don't, unless the sentence is long. German uses commas far more systematically than English — they mark the boundary between clauses, not a pause for breath.
*Sondern* is only used after a **negative** statement: *Ich trinke keinen Kaffee, **sondern** Tee.* Using *aber* here isn't wrong, but it sounds less precise.

head: German
English
Months
What it's like
rows: Es ist heiß und hell bis 22 Uhr.
Es regnet und es ist windig.
Es schneit und es wird früh dunkel.

blocks.text: All the seasons take *im*: *im Sommer*, *im Winter*. And one sentence you'll hear every December: ***Es wird schon um vier Uhr dunkel*** — it's dark by four in the afternoon. For anyone coming from near the equator, that's a much bigger shock than the temperature.

In Germany the weather isn't empty small talk but a perfectly valid way to open a conversation with anyone — a neighbor in the elevator, someone in line, a cashier. Master the six sentences below and you have a way into any conversation.

blocks.title: Practice linking sentences
items: Take two short sentences you already know and link them with each of the four conjunctions in turn — and notice how the meaning changes.
*Es ist kalt.* + *Ich bleibe zu Hause.* → *Es ist kalt, **denn**…* / *Es ist kalt, **aber**…* / *Es ist kalt **und**…*
Say them all out loud. What you're training isn't grammar knowledge but the habit of linking — that's what separates a beginner's sentences from a fluent speaker's.
Wie ist das Wetter heute?
Es regnet seit heute Morgen.
Im Januar ist es oft minus fünf Grad.
Es ist kalt, aber sonnig.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn es regnet.
Es wird früh dunkel.
Es ist kalt ____ es regnet.
Es ist kalt, ____ es ist sonnig.
Ich kaufe eine Jacke ____ ich bleibe zu Hause.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, ____ das Wetter ist schlecht.
Im Sommer ist es warm ____ hell.
Ich gehe nicht raus, ____ es schneit.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: das Wetter / wie / heute / ist
seit heute Morgen / es / regnet
sonnig / kalt / es ist / aber
zwei Jahreszeiten / es gibt / nur
dunkel / früh / es wird / im Winter
einen Regenschirm / mit / nimm

answers: What's the weather like today? — It's been raining since this morning. — In January it's often minus five degrees. — It's cold, but sunny. — I'm staying at home, because it's raining. — It gets dark early.
